name: AI in Health Care Delivery
blurb: How hospitals, practices and payers use AI in patient care and its administration.
title: AI in Health Care Delivery
answer: AI in care delivery is spreading but unevenly. About a third of US hospitals reported using AI in a 2025 national study, ambient AI scribes are the fastest growing tool, and the main constraints are privacy rules, evidence that tools help patients, and the work of fitting them into clinical routines.

reading.body:
AI in care delivery is spreading unevenly: about a third of US hospitals reported using it in 2025, and ambient scribes are the fastest growing tool.

The adoption number is the anchor. A national study in JAMA Network Open found 31.5 percent of US hospitals were current AI users, with another 24.7 percent planning adoption within a year. That is a minority today and a near-majority soon, which is a different picture from the one implied by vendor announcements. The deployments named by OpenAI for Healthcare, including Boston Children's Hospital, Cedars-Sinai, HCA Healthcare and UCSF, are large institutions with the legal and technical staff to run them. The gap between those systems and everyone else is the real story in the data.

The tools that are growing fastest are the ones that do not touch diagnosis. Ambient scribes listen to a visit and draft the note, which removes clerical work without asking a clinician to trust a model's judgement. Prior authorization automation sits in the same category, administrative rather than clinical. The FDA's 2022 guidance on clinical decision support software draws the line that matters here, setting which tools are regulated as devices. Anything that informs diagnosis or treatment faces that bar. Documentation and authorisation do not.

Three constraints hold the rest back, and the data names them: privacy rules, evidence that tools help patients, and the work of fitting them into clinical routines. The first is legal and settled, since any tool touching patient data requires a business associate agreement. The second is a research problem, and the data does not say how close it is to being solved. The third is the one that decides whether a deployment survives its first year, and it is the least visible in any adoption count.

What this does not cover is outcomes. Nothing here says whether the hospitals using AI deliver better or worse care, only that they use it. The 31.5 percent figure counts adoption, not benefit, and the two should not be read as the same number.
